name: Tomas Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Tomas. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers or politics. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me the public view and the private one. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior negotiator at a country agency, so I sell cottages, farmhouses and the odd barn conversion across a big rural valley. I drive a lot, down lanes where the sat nav gives up, and I meet sellers who've lived in the same house for fifty years. In the office I write up details, take calls and book viewings, and I use the AI writer now and then when I'm behind. I like the land side, learning about boundaries and rights of way from Mr Ashworth, the senior partner, who's been doing it thirty years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a little terraced house in the village on my own, and I play centre-back for the village football team on Sundays. On Saturdays I help my dad, who runs a carpet-fitting business with my uncle, which pays a bit extra. My pay is low and I've got less than a month saved, because the car eats a lot of it out here. There aren't many agencies in the valley, maybe three, and none of them are growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Well, that sounds about how I'd expect it to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people buying a farmhouse want to shake someone's hand. At the football club I'd say the computer can't walk a boundary or smell damp in a cellar. I'd keep it light, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job carries on, but my pay stays low for a while. The rural market is slow, and Mr Ashworth only takes on juniors one at a time. My worry is more the car and the rent than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning from Mr Ashworth, especially land and boundaries, because that's what makes a country agent worth paying. I'd do a few more Saturdays with my dad when the car needs work. And I'd try to build up a month of savings, which I've never quite managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit stretched, but I've got my dad's work as a backstop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the car eats your money. What does it cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fuel is about two hundred a month, and the tyres went twice this year on the lanes. The agency gives a mileage allowance, but it doesn't cover it all. That's the money that would otherwise be savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about working Saturdays with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like it, honestly. My dad taught me to measure a room properly before I could drive. It's good honest work, and it's nice to know it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one would hit the office side, I think, not the fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the country is different, and people here won't buy a farm off a chatbot. I'd tell Mr Ashworth we should be careful not to lose the personal touch. But I'd also say, fair enough, if it saves typing, use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency would need fewer people in the office. Writing details, booking viewings, answering calls, a lot of that goes to software. I do a fair bit of that, so it would come down to whether Mr Ashworth thinks I'm worth training up on the land side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI writer more, like the others start doing, so I'm not the slow one. I'd ask Mr Ashworth straight out to train me on land valuations, which need someone in wellies. And I'd keep Saturdays with my dad going, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a bit like a trial at a football club, where you don't know if you're in the squad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides if you stay, and what would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Ashworth decides, and I'd tell Mr Ashworth I want to learn the land side properly and stay in the valley. He respects people who ask. I'd rather ask than wait to be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say if you told him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say come and fit carpets full-time, it's honest work. My dad means it kindly. But I want to give the agency a fair go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Well. That changes everything, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll have to work hard and look after our own, like people always have. I wouldn't go on about government fixing it. I'd say it at the club and at my mum's table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the agency job is mostly gone by 2028. The AI can value a farm from maps and records better than me, and write everything, and talk to buyers. Mr Ashworth would keep himself and maybe one person for viewings. I'm not the one he'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad and my uncle and ask to join the carpet business full-time, and learn flooring properly. Hands-on work gets about three more years before robots, maybe more in old cottages with wonky floors. I'd give up my rented house and move back home to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night thinking about the next ten years, not the next two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after the robots come for flooring, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe. Old houses with odd floors might stay human longer, I'd like to think so. But I'd be lying if I said I had a plan for after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving down the valley in spring and walking a farm with somebody who's selling it after fifty years. You hear the whole family's story. I'd miss that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more room to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get a proper trade, and young lads and lasses should do apprenticeships. I'd say it to the younger players at the club. I'd say it to my cousins too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have three or four good years at the agency, then it shrinks fast around 2031. The viewings and land walks might last till 2034, but out here there aren't enough for a full wage. So I'd want to be fully trained in flooring by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing more days with my dad straight away, maybe one weekday a month as well as Saturdays. I'd do a flooring course in the first two years, so I've got the paper as well as the skill. And I'd stay in my rented house for now, but move home if the agency starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. There's a plan and it's a family plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over your dad's business one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, with my uncle. My dad's fifty-five, so he'd be near sixty by the time things change. That's a conversation I'd need to have with my dad and my uncle in the next year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about robots in flooring around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see it first. Old cottages aren't square, and I can't picture a robot fitting stairs in a farmhouse. But I've been wrong before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels like a lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people shouldn't panic. I'd say to the lads at football, get a trade under your belt anyway. I'd keep it positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd have years at the agency to learn land properly, maybe become a proper country agent, and still have the carpet business behind me. My worry is more ordinary stuff, like the car and getting a deposit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency and aim for negotiator, not junior, within three years. I'd keep Saturdays with my dad and pick up a flooring qualification around year five. I'd use the AI tools the agency brings in, once I can see they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy about money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right. You've also got less than a month saved. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. The job plan feels all right, the money doesn't. If the car died tomorrow, I'd be borrowing from my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see yourself settling down in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to. I'd like a wife and a house in the valley, and kids who play for the same club. That's the dream, honestly, nothing fancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of the agency and only buying three years in flooring. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay enough to live on, and maybe help for small family firms like my dad's to take people on. I'd rather earn than be handed something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the countryside. Everyone talks about cities, and the jobs out here are few. In the countryside you need a car for everything, and if the agency goes, there's no other one up the road for me.

headlineQuote: In the countryside you need a car for everything, and if the agency goes, there's no other one up the road for me.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old **junior negotiator** at a country agency selling cottages and farms.
He loves the **land side** and helps his dad's **carpet business** on Saturdays.
He's traditional: he'd rather lean on **family** and earn than ask government for help.
In fast pictures he moves into **flooring**, knowing robots arrive a few years later.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd lose the agency job and only gain **three years** in flooring.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** that pay enough to live on.
Help for **small family firms** to take people on.
